nameStory: These tiny fungi earned their enchanting name from their perfect cup shape and bright yellow color that looks like miniature fairy dinnerware scattered through the forest. The alternative name 'lemon discos' captures both their citrusy hue and flat, circular appearance when viewed from above.
description: Yellow Fairy Cups are minuscule fungi that produce bright yellow, cup-shaped fruiting bodies on rotting wood. Each tiny cup measures only about 1/8 inch across - so small you could easily walk past dozens without noticing them. They typically appear in clusters or groups, creating little colonies of sunshine-colored cups on bare, decaying hardwood logs and branches.

idTips.label: Tiny Yellow Cups
idTips.description: Look for bright lemon-yellow cups about 1/8 inch across with smooth, waxy surfaces that catch the light like tiny bowls

idTips.label: Clustered Growth
idTips.description: Usually found in groups or dense clusters rather than solitary specimens, creating patches of yellow dots

idTips.label: Bare Hardwood Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on decaying deciduous wood that has lost its bark, never on bark-covered or coniferous wood

idTips.label: Sessile Attachment
idTips.description: Cups sit directly on the wood surface without visible stalks, appearing to emerge straight from the substrate

idTips.label: Smooth Texture
idTips.description: Surfaces feel waxy and smooth to gentle touch, not fuzzy or rough like many other small fungi

idTips.label: Late Season Timing
idTips.description: Most abundant in late summer through autumn when other small cup fungi may be less common

habitat: Look for Yellow Fairy Cups on rotting hardwood logs, branches, and stumps in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. They prefer wood that has lost its bark and is well into the decay process, often found on maple, oak, birch, and other broadleaf trees. You'll find them from sea level to mountain elevations wherever suitable decaying hardwood is present.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in spring as they prefer the later growing season for fruiting.
seasonality.summer: May begin appearing in late summer, especially during humid periods following rain.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for fruiting, when fresh yellow cups are most abundant and easily spotted against darkening wood.
seasonality.winter: Old, dried specimens may persist but are usually faded and less recognizable.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny - you could fit about 200 of these fairy cups across a single dollar bill - Yellow Fairy Cups are found on every continent except Antarctica, making them one of the most widely distributed fungi on Earth.
confusionNotes: Several other small cup fungi look similar, but most differ in color (orange, white, or brown instead of bright yellow) or grow on different substrates like bark or coniferous wood. Remember: bright yellow + bare hardwood + tiny size = Yellow Fairy Cups.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Calycina' comes from the Greek word for cup or chalice, while 'citrina' refers to the citrus-like yellow color. Despite being called 'fairy cups,' these fungi play a very real ecological role as decomposers, helping break down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
compareHints: Yellow Fairy Cups are the only species in their genus found in New England, making them unique among their close relatives. They can be distinguished from other small cup fungi in the Pezizellaceae family by their consistently bright yellow color and exclusive preference for bark-free hardwood substrates. Most similar species are either different colors or grow on bark, needles, or other materials.
